compatibility.lead: Much of Ori Studio is a careful port of work the community already built — Oriedita, TreeMaker and Box Pleating Studio — and keeping import and export interoperability with those tools is a commitment.
compatibility.title: Built on the tools you already use

bp.body: Lay flaps out on a grid, with rivers, stretch devices and symmetry constraints, and read the crease pattern off the packing.
bp.figureAlt: Flaps packed onto a box-pleating grid with its crease pattern alongside.
bp.title: Box Pleating

explori.body: Send your tree to Brandon Wong's searchable archive of 22.5° crease patterns and browse the closest matches it returns.
explori.figureAlt: A grid of 22.5° crease patterns returned from an ExplOri search.
explori.title: ExplOri

design.lead: Pack your model with whichever method suits it, with several designs open side by side in tabs. Each one builds a crease pattern you can send straight to the editor.
design.title: A tabbed design workspace

treemaker.body: Sketch a tree, set edge lengths and strain, and let the optimizer pack circles and rivers into a base.
treemaker.figureAlt: A tree structure beside the circle packing the optimizer found for it.
treemaker.title: Circle Packing

angles.body: Draw, simulate, and solve origami models with non-flat creases.
angles.figureAlt: A crease pattern with fold-angle labels on its creases.
angles.title: Support for non-flat creases

diagnostics.body: Kawasaki and Maekawa where the paper folds flat. Where it does not, each vertex is checked in three dimensions — walking its creases around to see whether the folds close back up, and by how far they miss.
diagnostics.figureAlt: Foldability diagnostics marking problem vertices on a crease pattern.
diagnostics.title: Foldability you can check as you go

edit.lead: Draw with a full set of construction and transform tools, snapped to the grid and to angles, and see foldability problems the moment you make them. Reference photos, notes and a folded preview all live on the same canvas.

media.body: Put a reference photo of the subject next to the paper and annotate the canvas with rich text. Both are saved with the project and dropped cleanly when you export to a format that has no room for them.
media.figureAlt: A reference photo and a text annotation placed beside a crease pattern.
media.title: Rich Images and Text

share.body: Send someone a crease pattern as a URL. They open it in their browser with nothing to install.
share.figureAlt: The share-link dialog with a copyable URL.
share.title: Share a pattern with a link

edit.title: An editor that keeps up

get.lead: Scroll back up and start a crease pattern — that is the whole setup. Discord is the best place to report a bug or suggest something, and where new work is announced first.
get.title: It runs in the browser. Nothing to install.

mobileHero.tagline: Design, edit and fold origami, all in the browser.

simulate.figureAlt: A folded 3D model simulating inline beside its crease pattern.
simulate.lead: Open a simulation in a window right next to the crease pattern you are drawing, so checking an idea costs a glance instead of a round trip through another program. A full Simulate workspace is there when you want the model on its own.
simulate.title: Fold it without leaving the pattern

what.figureAlt: The Ori Studio workspace: a crease pattern on the canvas with the tool rail and inspector panels around it.
what.lead: Sketch a base, draw the crease pattern, and fold it to see whether it works — in one place, in the browser, with nothing to install and no account.
what.title: A free, open-source workspace for origami design
